name: Badger
attack_signs: Coop doors, panels or weak wire torn open by force
Deep digging under fences
Birds eaten on site, with parts left and heavy disturbance
Eggs eaten
what_they_take: Adult birds and eggs. Can break into poorly built coops.
prevention: Build a strong coop with solid timber and secure fixings.
Stop digging with a buried wire apron or skirt, about 12 inches (30 cm) down or laid flat outward along the base of the run.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
Electric poultry netting or offset electric wires around the run are very effective.

name: Bears
attack_signs: Coop, fence or feed store badly smashed
Feed bins opened and emptied
Birds and eggs gone, with heavy damage everywhere
what_they_take: Feed first, then birds and eggs. Black bears are the usual culprit.
prevention: Electric fencing around coop and run.
Store feed in metal bins and remove feeders at night.
Do not leave kitchen scraps or compost near the coop.

name: Bobcat
attack_signs: One bird taken, sometimes cached under leaves or debris nearby
Bite marks to the head and neck
Can climb or jump fences
what_they_take: Usually one adult bird at a time.
prevention: Cover the run with a solid roof or mesh.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.

name: Cats (domestic and feral)
attack_signs: Chicks or small bantams missing or partly eaten, often starting at the head
Adult full-size hens are usually left alone
Feathers scattered near cover
what_they_take: Chicks, young birds and bantams. Rarely adult large-fowl hens.
prevention: Keep chicks in a covered brooder or pen.
Cover the run with a solid roof or mesh.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.

name: Coyote
attack_signs: Whole birds taken and carried off, few remains
Scattered feathers where the bird was caught
May jump or dig under fences
Daytime attacks are common where coyotes are used to people
what_they_take: One or more adult birds, usually carried away.
prevention: Electric poultry netting or offset electric wires around the run are very effective.
Stop digging with a buried wire apron or skirt, about 12 inches (30 cm) down or laid flat outward along the base of the run.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
A tall fence (about 6 feet) with an outward overhang or electric top wire.

sources.publisher: Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management

name: Crows, ravens and magpies
attack_signs: Eggs missing, or shells with a hole pecked in and contents gone
Shells carried away and found some distance from the nest
Chicks taken from open runs
what_they_take: Eggs and chicks.
prevention: Collect eggs at least daily.
Put nest boxes inside the coop, out of sight.
Cover the run with a solid roof or mesh.

sources.publisher: Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management

name: Dogs
attack_signs: Many birds killed or badly mauled but not eaten
Feathers everywhere and signs of a chase
Fence damage or digging at the base
Bodies scattered around the yard
what_they_take: Several birds at once, often killed but left.
prevention: A strong perimeter fence.
Electric poultry netting or offset electric wires around the run are very effective.
Talk to neighbours about loose dogs. In the UK, dog attacks on poultry can be reported to the police.

sources.publisher: Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management

name: Eagles
attack_signs: Whole bird carried away with no remains
A few feathers where the bird was grabbed
Talon punctures on the back if a bird escapes
what_they_take: Adult birds carried away. Bald and golden eagles are protected by law.
prevention: Cover the run with a solid roof or mesh.
Provide shrubs, covered areas or shelters birds can run under.
All eagles and hawks are protected in the US and UK. Only non-lethal prevention is allowed.

name: Red fox
attack_signs: One or more birds missing, often taken away whole
Clumps of feathers where birds were caught, sometimes a feather trail
Several birds killed at once if the fox gets into the coop (surplus killing)
Bodies sometimes cached or buried
Digging under fences
what_they_take: Adult birds, usually carried off. May kill many if trapped in with them.
prevention: Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
Electric poultry netting or offset electric wires around the run are very effective.
Stop digging with a buried wire apron or skirt, about 12 inches (30 cm) down or laid flat outward along the base of the run.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
Foxes also hunt in daylight in spring and summer when feeding cubs.

sources.publisher: Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management

name: Hawks
attack_signs: Bird killed in the open run or yard during the day
Feathers plucked, with a scatter or pile of feathers around the body
Breast meat eaten on the spot
Talon puncture wounds on the back and head
Small birds and chicks may be carried off
what_they_take: Chicks, bantams and some adult hens. In the UK, goshawks, sparrowhawks and buzzards occasionally take poultry.
prevention: Cover the run with a solid roof or mesh.
Provide cover such as shrubs or a shelter to hide under.
A rooster can give warning calls.
All hawks are protected in the US and UK. Only non-lethal prevention is allowed.

sources.publisher: Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management

name: Hedgehogs
attack_signs: Eggs broken and eaten in nest boxes at ground level
Messy shell fragments left behind
what_they_take: Eggs. They do not harm adult birds.
prevention: Collect eggs at least daily.
Raise nest boxes off the ground.
Hedgehogs are a declining protected species. Keep them out, never harm them.

name: Mink
attack_signs: Several birds killed at once
Bite wounds to the head and neck
Bodies piled or dragged into a corner or hole
Usually near water
what_they_take: Several birds in one attack. American mink is also a feral invasive species in the UK.
prevention: Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
Seal every gap larger than about 1 inch (2.5 cm), including where walls meet the floor and roof.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.

name: Opossum
attack_signs: One bird killed inside the coop, often partly eaten from the belly or vent
Messy scene
Eggs eaten, shells left crushed in the nest
Chicks taken
what_they_take: Eggs, chicks and sometimes a single adult bird.
prevention: Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
Collect eggs at least daily.
Store feed in metal bins and remove feeders at night.

name: Owls
attack_signs: Bird taken from an open run or tree roost at night
Head and neck eaten, rest of the body left
Feathers scattered around the body
Great horned owls can take full-size hens
what_they_take: Birds roosting outside or in open-top runs. In the US, great horned owls are the main threat.
prevention: Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
Cover the run with a solid roof or mesh.
Do not let birds roost in trees or on open fences.
Owls are protected in the US and UK.

name: Pine marten
attack_signs: Several birds killed, often bites to the head or neck
Can climb well and enter through small gaps high up
Bodies may be cached
what_they_take: Birds and eggs. Pine martens are rare and legally protected in the UK.
prevention: Seal every gap larger than about 1 inch (2.5 cm), including where walls meet the floor and roof.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.

name: Polecat
attack_signs: Several birds killed at once
Bites to the back of the head and neck
Bodies stored or cached together
what_they_take: Several birds in one visit, and eggs.
prevention: Seal every gap larger than about 1 inch (2.5 cm), including where walls meet the floor and roof.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.

name: Raccoon
attack_signs: Birds pulled through wire, with heads or legs missing
Head and crop eaten, breast torn open
Several birds killed in one night
Eggs eaten, shells left nearby
Latches and doors opened
what_they_take: Adult birds, chicks and eggs.
prevention: Use two-step latches or carabiners. Simple hooks and turn buttons can be opened.
Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.
Chicken wire is easily torn by raccoons.

name: Rats
attack_signs: Eggs disappear without trace or are rolled away
Chicks missing or dragged into burrows
Bites to the feet, legs or backs of sleeping birds
Burrows near the coop and droppings in feed
what_they_take: Eggs, chicks and feed. Rarely kill adults but can wound them.
prevention: Store feed in metal bins and remove feeders at night.
Collect eggs at least daily.
Build on a solid floor or bury mesh under the coop.
Clear spilled feed daily.

Chicks killed and partly eaten
Musky smell around the coop
Shallow digging around the coop
what_they_take: Mainly eggs and chicks. Rarely adults.
prevention: Collect eggs at least daily.
Stop digging with a buried wire apron or skirt, about 12 inches (30 cm) down or laid flat outward along the base of the run.
Shut birds in a secure coop every night before dusk. An automatic door helps.

prevention: Use 1/2 inch (12 to 13 mm) welded wire mesh, not chicken wire, on runs and vents. Chicken wire keeps chickens in but does not keep predators out.
